voiceInstructions: Warm, precise American English mathematics teacher. Read factorials, choices and restrictions clearly. Brief natural pauses after questions. Speak every final sentence. Do not add material absent from the script.
title: Permutations and combinations: count choices, order and restrictions

chapters.title: Choose the addition rule or multiplication rule
chapters.formula: Disjoint alternatives: m+n; successive choices: m×n
points: Define exactly what counts as one outcome.
Add mutually exclusive cases.
Multiply valid successive choices, splitting into cases when their counts differ.
chapters.script: Counting begins by defining an outcome. If you choose one shirt, one pair of trousers and one pair of shoes, an outfit is the complete triple of choices. With two shirts, three trousers and two shoe options, there are two times three times two, or twelve outfits. This multiplication rule works because each partial choice admits the stated number of next choices. It does not require probability independence. If restrictions make that number vary, split into cases or count each branch separately. The addition rule combines disjoint alternatives. If a journey uses either one of four train services or one of three bus services, and the services are distinct options, there are seven choices. You add because taking one service is the outcome; you are not taking a train and then a bus. If cases overlap, simple addition double counts the shared outcomes. Remove that overlap or rewrite the cases so each outcome belongs to exactly one. A small tree diagram is useful: branches represent successive choices, and completed paths represent outcomes. Before using a factorial or a combination symbol, say whether you are selecting, ordering or performing several stages.

chapters.title: Count ordered selections using permutations
points: Objects are distinct and selected without replacement.
Each ranked position is a different role.
Factorials describe nonnegative integer counts in this class.
chapters.script: Suppose seven distinct runners compete for first, second and third positions, with no ties. A podium is an ordered list of three different people. There are seven choices for first, six for second and five for third, giving two hundred ten podiums. This is the permutation count P of seven, three. For n distinct objects placed into r ordered positions without replacement, multiply n by n minus one, continuing for r factors. In factorial notation the result is n factorial divided by n minus r factorial. A factorial multiplies positive integers down to one, and zero factorial is defined as one. This is consistent with one empty arrangement when no positions are filled. Arranging all n distinct objects gives n factorial. Choosing zero positions gives one outcome, not zero. The formula assumes r is an integer between zero and n. If more distinct objects are requested than are available without replacement, there are no such arrangements. When repetition is allowed instead, each position may have n choices and the count becomes n to the power r. Always attach the replacement rule and the meaning of positions to the formula. A selection of three people with no assigned roles is a different outcome from a ranked podium.

chapters.title: Count unordered selections and derive combination identities
points: An unordered subset ignores internal order.
Each r-element subset produces r! ordered lists.
Pascal’s identity splits cases by one distinguished object.
chapters.script: A committee of three chosen from seven distinct people has no ranking among its members. Listing the same three names in a different order does not create a different committee. The permutation count two hundred ten counts each committee three factorial times, because its members can occupy the three list positions in six orders. Divide by six to obtain thirty five committees. In general, C of n, r equals n factorial divided by r factorial times n minus r factorial. The relation P of n, r equals r factorial times C of n, r explains the distinction between selection and arrangement. Selecting r people is also equivalent to specifying the n minus r people left out, giving C of n, r equal to C of n, n minus r. Pascal's identity follows by fixing one distinguished person. A committee either contains that person and chooses its remaining r minus one members from the others, or excludes that person and chooses all r from the others. The cases are disjoint. Thus C of n, r is C of n minus one, r minus one plus C of n minus one, r. For choosing three from seven, this gives fifteen plus twenty, again thirty five.

chapters.title: Arrange objects with repeated types
points: Repeated copies of a type are indistinguishable.
Divide out only permutations that leave the visible outcome unchanged.
Check multiplicities before evaluating factorials.
chapters.script: Repeated symbols change the meaning of an arrangement. The word BANANA contains six letters: three copies of A, two copies of N and one B. If every physical copy were temporarily labelled, six factorial orders would be possible. Removing labels makes each visible arrangement occur three factorial times from the A labels and two factorial times from the N labels. Divide by both factors to obtain sixty distinct strings. More generally, with n objects divided into indistinguishable types of multiplicities n one, n two and so on, the count is n factorial divided by the product of the multiplicity factorials. The multiplicities must sum to n. For A, A, B, the visible strings are AAB, ABA and BAA, agreeing with three factorial divided by two factorial. Do not divide by a factorial merely because two objects share a broad description if the problem treats those objects as distinct. Two named students remain distinct even if they wear identical uniforms. Conversely, labelling identical balls changes a distribution problem. The right divisor comes from how many labelled outcomes collapse to each visible outcome. Check that this number is constant before using division as a shortcut. This keeps repeated object reasoning connected to the actual objects being counted.

chapters.title: Use blocks to enforce adjacency
chapters.formula: Two specified people adjacent in a 5-person row: 2!×4!=48
points: Treat a required adjacent group as one unit.
Count arrangements inside the block separately.
Check that the block construction counts each valid row once.
chapters.script: Adjacency constraints often become simpler when a group is treated as one block. Five distinct people, including A and B, stand in a row. If A and B must be adjacent, combine them into one block. Along with the other three people, this makes four units to arrange, giving four factorial orders. Inside the block, A B and B A are two different orders. Multiply to obtain forty eight rows. If three specified people among the same five must all stand consecutively, the block and two remaining people form three units. There are three factorial outer orders and three factorial internal orders, giving thirty six rows. The phrase together must mean consecutive positions for this construction. It does not automatically mean a fixed internal order; that needs a separate condition. If a particular order A before B is required within their two person block, only one internal order remains. Blocks may also fail when several adjacency requirements overlap, so draw the intended pattern before multiplying. A useful check for the two person example is that all five person rows number one hundred twenty. The forty eight adjacent rows form a subset, leaving seventy two rows where A and B are separated. We will recover that separated count with gaps.

chapters.title: Use gaps to prevent selected neighbours
points: Arrange the anchor objects first.
Choose different gaps for objects that must be separated.
Arrange the distinct special objects within the selected gaps.
chapters.script: To keep two specified people apart in a five person row, arrange the other three people first. There are three factorial anchor orders. Each anchor row has four gaps: before the first person, between consecutive people and after the last. Put the two special people into different gaps, choosing two of the four gaps in six ways. Then decide which special person uses which chosen gap in two ways. The result is six times six times two, or seventy two rows. Each valid row has a unique anchor order and choice of occupied gaps, so no row is counted twice. This agrees with subtracting the forty eight adjacent rows from all one hundred twenty rows. The same method handles four distinct anchors and three distinct special people when no two specials may be neighbours. Four factorial anchor orders give five gaps; choose three gaps and arrange the three specials, giving four factorial times C of five, three times three factorial, or one thousand four hundred forty. If specials are indistinguishable, remove their internal arrangement factor. If several may share a gap, the simple different gap formula is unavailable. The wording of the separation condition determines which placement pattern is valid.

chapters.title: Specify what makes circular arrangements equivalent
chapters.formula: n distinct people around an unlabelled circle: (n−1)!
points: Rotations are identified in this model.
Reflections remain different unless explicitly identified.
Labelled chairs restore the ordinary n! count.
chapters.script: Circular arrangements require an equivalence convention. Suppose six distinct people sit around a round table, with rotations treated as the same seating and reflections treated as different. Fix one chosen person as the reference position. The other five can be placed clockwise in five factorial orders, giving one hundred twenty circular seatings. This removes the rotational overcount that would appear if we numbered all six starting positions. If the chairs are labelled, rotations change which labelled chair each person occupies, so there are six factorial seat assignments instead. Do not automatically divide by another factor of two: clockwise and anticlockwise orders are different under the stated convention. Necklaces or bracelets can use different conventions, especially when repeated objects create additional symmetries. Those require a separate analysis. If A and B among the six people must be adjacent, treat them as a block. The block plus the other four people gives five units around the table. Fix a reference unit to count four factorial circular orders, then multiply by two internal block orders, obtaining forty eight. Always name the objects, decide whether chairs are labelled, and state whether reflection is identified before selecting a circular counting formula. The formula follows from those choices rather than from the word circle alone.

chapters.title: Count digit strings and numbers with a leading-zero rule
points: A number cannot start with zero.
A fixed-length code may permit leading zero.
Split even-number cases according to whether the units digit is zero.
chapters.script: A digit string and a three digit number need not have the same count. Using zero, one, two, three and four without repetition, a three digit number has four choices for its first digit because zero is excluded. After choosing a nonzero first digit, four digits remain, including zero, for the second position. Three remain for the third. The total is forty eight. A length three code allowing an initial zero instead has five times four times three, or sixty possibilities. If repetition is allowed for a three digit number, the count is four times five times five, or one hundred. To count even three digit numbers without repeated digits, split by the final digit. If it is zero, the first digit has four choices and the middle digit three, giving twelve. If the last digit is two or four, there are two choices for that last position. The first digit must exclude zero and the chosen last digit, leaving three choices. Then three digits remain for the middle position, giving eighteen. Add the disjoint cases to obtain thirty. Filling a constrained position first often makes the available choices easier to track. State the digit set and repetition rule throughout the argument.

chapters.title: Select constrained committees and then assign roles
chapters.formula: From 5 women and 4 men: at least one woman in a 3-person committee = C(9,3)−C(4,3)=80
points: Committee membership alone is unordered.
Use complement counting for at least one.
Roles assigned after selection introduce an arrangement factor.
chapters.script: A committee usually records who belongs, not the order in which names were chosen. From five distinct women and four distinct men, the total number of three person committees is C of nine, three, or eighty four. To require at least one woman, subtract the committees containing only men. There are C of four, three, or four of those, leaving eighty committees. The complement condition none is simpler than adding separate cases for one, two and three women. For exactly two women and one man, choose two from the five women and one from the four men. Multiply ten by four to obtain forty committees. Now suppose any three people may form a committee, but one of them must be designated chair. Choose the committee in eighty four ways and choose its chair in three ways, giving two hundred fifty two outcomes. Equivalently, choose the chair first in nine ways and the other two members from the remaining eight in twenty eight ways. The results agree because they describe the same final outcome. If several distinct roles are assigned, record which person fills each role. A committee with a chair is different from a committee with no roles, even when the same people belong to it.

chapters.title: Translate identical-object distributions into nonnegative solutions
points: Boxes are labelled and objects are identical in this model.
A bar separates the counts assigned to neighbouring boxes.
Positive requirements are handled by assigning one object first.
chapters.script: A distribution problem must say whether the objects and boxes are distinguishable. Consider five identical balls placed into three labelled boxes, allowing an empty box. An outcome is completely described by nonnegative integers x, y and z whose sum is five. Write five stars and insert two bars to split them into three groups. A group may be empty, so bars may be adjacent or occur at either end. Choosing the two bar positions among seven total positions gives C of seven, two, or twenty one distributions. This is the stars and bars argument for a finite nonnegative integer solution count. If every box must receive at least one ball, place one ball in each box first. Two balls remain to distribute without restrictions. There are C of four, two, or six possibilities. Equivalently, positive x, y, z become one plus three new nonnegative variables. If the five balls were distinct instead, each independently chooses one of the three labelled boxes, giving three to the fifth power, or two hundred forty three assignments when empty boxes are allowed. Neither count applies automatically to unlabelled boxes. Before choosing a formula, state the object types, box labels and lower bounds so the combinatorial model matches the question.

quiz.question: With 2 shirts, 3 trousers and 2 shoe choices, the number of outfits choosing one of each is:
quiz.explanation: An outfit is a triple of successive choices. Multiply 2×3×2=12; addition would count individual options rather than complete outfits.

quiz.question: A traveller chooses exactly one of 4 train services or 3 distinct bus services. The number of choices is:
quiz.explanation: The alternatives are disjoint and exactly one service is chosen, so the addition principle gives 4+3=7 distinct choices.

quiz.question: Seven distinct runners fill first, second and third places without ties. The number of podiums is:
quiz.explanation: Ranked places make order matter and each runner is used at most once. Thus P(7,3)=7×6×5=210 possible podiums.

quiz.question: The value of 0! is:
quiz.explanation: There is one empty arrangement of no objects. Defining 0!=1 also makes P(n,n)=n! and C(n,0)=1 consistent with their counts.

quiz.question: The number of unordered 3-person committees from 7 distinct people is:
quiz.explanation: The committee has no ranked positions. Divide P(7,3)=210 by the 3!=6 orders of each selected triple, obtaining 35.

quiz.question: For 0≤r≤n, P(n,r) equals:
quiz.explanation: Every unordered r-element selection gives exactly r! ordered lists, so P(n,r)=r!C(n,r) for distinct objects without replacement.

quiz.question: How many distinct strings use all letters of BANANA?
quiz.explanation: There are six letters with three indistinguishable As and two indistinguishable Ns. The count is 6!/(3!2!)=60.

quiz.question: The distinct arrangements of A,A,B number:
quiz.explanation: The visible strings are AAB, ABA and BAA. Equivalently, divide 3! by the 2! permutations of the indistinguishable As.

quiz.question: Five distinct people stand in a row. Two specified people must be adjacent in either order. The count is:
quiz.explanation: Treat the pair as a block, giving four units to arrange in 4! ways. Multiply by the two internal pair orders to get 48.

quiz.question: Five distinct people stand in a row. Three specified people must be consecutive in any internal order. The count is:
quiz.explanation: The three-person block and the other two people form three units. There are 3! outer orders and 3! internal block orders, giving 36.

quiz.question: Five distinct people stand in a row. Two specified people must not be adjacent. The count is:
quiz.explanation: All rows number 5!=120. Adjacent rows number 2×4!=48. The required complement is 120−48=72.

quiz.question: Four distinct anchors and three distinct specials form a row with no neighbouring specials. The count is:
quiz.explanation: Arrange the anchors in 4! ways, choose three of the five gaps, and order the specials in 3! ways: 24×10×6=1440.

quiz.question: Six distinct people sit around an unlabelled round table. Rotations are identical and reflections distinct. The count is:
quiz.explanation: Fix one person to remove rotational duplication. The other five have 5!=120 clockwise orders; reflections are not identified.

quiz.question: Six distinct people occupy six labelled chairs. The number of assignments is:
quiz.explanation: Chair labels distinguish rotations, so each full seat assignment is an ordinary permutation of six people: 6!=720.

quiz.question: Using {0,1,2,3,4} without repetition, how many 3-digit numbers are possible?
quiz.explanation: The first digit has four nonzero choices; then four digits remain for the second place and three for the last. The product is 48.

quiz.question: Using {0,1,2,3,4} without repetition, how many even 3-digit numbers are possible?
quiz.explanation: Ending in zero gives 4×3=12. Ending in 2 or 4 gives 2×3×3=18. The disjoint cases sum to 30.

quiz.question: From 5 distinct women and 4 distinct men, how many 3-person committees contain at least one woman?
quiz.explanation: Subtract all-male committees from all committees: C(9,3)−C(4,3)=84−4=80. At least one includes committees with two or three women.

quiz.question: From 5 distinct women and 4 distinct men, how many committees contain exactly 2 women and 1 man?
quiz.explanation: Choose two of the five women and one of the four men: C(5,2)C(4,1)=10×4=40, without assigning committee roles.

quiz.question: The number of nonnegative integer triples satisfying x+y+z=5 is:
quiz.explanation: Five stars and two bars give C(7,2)=21 possibilities. Empty groups are allowed, matching the nonnegative condition.

quiz.question: The number of positive integer triples satisfying x+y+z=5 is:
quiz.explanation: Assign one unit to each variable first. The remaining two units have C(2+3−1,3−1)=C(4,2)=6 nonnegative distributions.
